column2: Excellent choice for introduction to a new language
column3: Excellent choice for basic begineers.  Its great because of the variety of skills being used.  I also love using it with my grandkids. It offers short lessons where they can see immediate progress.
Simple to use.  Nice to hear proper pronunciation.  Appreciate this free app.

I am trying to learn Japanese, and I thought this would help me. Sadly when I opened it I saw it wasn't there. But it was great for the languages it does have! Therefore I am giving it 5 stars. I sure hope Japanese will be included in the next update.
My grandparents were Italian. I heard them speak, but never took the time to learn myself. Now I am learning and love it. It's a good program, but I wouldn't call it easy. It is effective.
A Great Free way to learn another language

I'm on level 3 French, and I already love this app and the computer version. It makes learning easy and you only need to do one lesson a day. You can also strengthen your skills. There are many languages, from Spanish to Irish to the upcoming Greek and Klingon! So definitely get this app. I've heard to get through the entire language, it takes about 1-3 months, as you learn words chunks at a time. 11/10 stars.

I've tried Duolingo both to review a language learned decades ago, and to start from nothing on a new language. For review, it's fabulous. For a totally new language, I couldn't do it with the app by itself. The website version has additional information (rules) that help, but still not quite enough for me without some kind of textbook approach.

column2: Fun and interesting way to learn
column3: I find this a fun and interesting was to learn a new language, I'm working on German but I wish they had Pennsylvania German also. I travel to Amish areas from time to time and would enjoy conversations with them.

This is by far my favorite language learning app out of the ones I have tried. It plays like a game, not like those boring flashcards apps so often rely on. I think they could do so much more with their Lingot reward system, but that isn't the focus so it does not affect my rating. I have learned SO MUCH using Duolingo!  I have rocketed from a year and a half of slow classes (11 years ago) to an estimated 50% fluency in a matter of months, just messing around on the app or web page in my spare time. I could not ask for a better learning aid!

column2: a simple intro to language learning
column3: This app is useful for simple communication.  I have completed the entire program and still use it for practice.  There is no didactic teaching but you can pick up some useful  grammatical advice from user's comments.  You really need more formal language instruction to achieve any fluency.

Love, love, love this app! The best way to learn a language and it's free!  I got this to brush up on my Spanish and German (which I hadn't put to use in years) and have started learning Portuguese too.  There are modules for native speakers of a number of languages, not just English, and they keep adding new modules.It works like a game and is very addictive - you progress through different levels, earning points along the way.  As you pass certain checkpoints, new levels are unlocked. You practice translating things you hear, translating what you read (both to and from your native language), and in most modules are tested on your pronunciation also.  You can either work on learning something new, or practice lessons you've already done (choose one where you feel you need help, or let them choose.) If you go on their website, you can also practice reading and translating articles and play against other users.Minor gripes:1) They used to have the option to play other users (or their automated "Duobot")  from the app and removed it in the latest update :(.2) It would be nice if they could find more things to "shop" for with your points - the selection is very limited and unimaginative.3) I'd like to see them add a reference section with some basic grammar and pronunciation "rules", standard verb conjugation, etc. for the language.  You can learn very effectively without them, but sometimes seeing everything written out can provide the "aha!" moment to get you past a bump in the learning process.But I like this enough that it isn't even worth removing a star.  I'm finally getting my German articles correct (most of the time) - something 4 years of College and some native speakers in my family didn't do for me. This app rocks!

column2: Duolingo is the app for me!
column3: I this app it run perfectly on my K.F. hd7! I love that it allows you to chat with other people because if you need a deeper definition you can leave a comment on the question and someone can answer. I also like that they are split up into categories so everything isn't all jumbled up! Overall, it is great app that I have learned a lot from.

i love this program! the way it teaches you language is fun and easy and a bit of a challenge. i mean you get to learn to read write (type) and speak a language all at once. and this was waaaay more affordable than rosetta stone and probably works the same way. DONT EVER TAKE THIS AWAY! i would be very upset because i love this program so much. one suggestion though: add more languages

Duolingo is fun.  I took Spanish way back in high school and thought it time to refresh.  Duolingo provides a great experience allowing you to hear, speak, read and write in the language of choice.  In addition it offers an opportunity to share the experience with others.

I love duolingo! I am learning french, german, and spanish!  And after only a couple months, I am already 40% fluent in french! (And even critique your english!)All in all I think this is the best choice for anyone who wants to learn a language!

column2: Best app for learning new languages
column3: Duolingo is the best app for learning new languages! It helped me pronounce the words and phrases correctly and when I didnt understand, it made it easy to get back on track. Duolingo is the most motivating language course I've ever seen.  It feels like a game, and is designed to keep you moving forward.  It is also concise and surprisingly comprehensive.  Each part has a lesson to read at the beginning, and if you don't understand why you got an answer wrong, there are discussion boards for each and every question.  So far I have not had a question I could not get the answer to, and I am almost halfway through.  I especially like how it encourages me to go back and strengthen skills in constant review.  This ensures that what I learn will eventually get written in my long term memory, its just a matter of time and consistency.  Anybody who uses Duolingo frequently, consistently, and for a long period of time (at least a year) will learn a new language.  Go ahead and get the answers wrong as often as you need to.  The algorithms are designed to program the human brain and you will eventually find yourself getting answers right in spite of yourself, even if you don't quite understand the grammatical principles behind it all.  Duolingo is built on principles of positive reinforcement, making it easier to persevere.  I use it in conjunction with short stories written in the language I'm trying to learn, and movies also in the language with English subtitles.  In only a month, I am understanding so much morevthan I ever thought possible.  I can't believe its free.  Its better than programs I've paid good money for.

column3: I am just learning Spanish, & this app has been a fun way to learn a new language. You have to remember that it's FREE - so you're not going to be speaking like a native in a month or two. Some of the reviews about the app leave me wondering that people expect too much for nothing. If you want to really learn a language - YOU have to WORK HARD at it! I have been doing this Duolingo app, plus the "Spanish in a Month" app. everyday for an hour. Between the 2 apps, I prefer this one. I like how it repeats the words, sentences, & puts pictures with the words. It also has you translate the words or sentences in English or what the Spanish equivalent of the same is. By "emersion, visualization/hearing - remembering a word with a picture & hearing over again," you will retain it.I also recommend watching some TV or internet in the language you are learning or if you know someone who is fluent in that language, have them help you & speak to you only in their native tongue. I have a friend who is Spanish & she has been a HUGE help with helping me on tougher sentence forms or quizzing me on words when I am not on the Duolingo! (You'd be surprised how much you may know/not know when you are NOT on the program...and I HIGHLY encourage you to try this to see how much you have retained...it's the way to know how far you are coming along if you are serious about learning a language!!Hope this helps!

column2: Duolingo is an awesome way to learn and practice new languages
column3: No two ways about it, Duolingo is an awesome way to learn and practice new languages. If you already have some education (say, old high school classes you wish you'd taken more seriously), it offers an assessment to put you at the right level, considering what you might already know. Duolingo breaks everything down into lessons that build upon each other, and prompts you to practice as you go, returning to older lessons to cement them while learning new words and grammar. Having used Rosetta Stone several times in the past, I think that Duolingo's program is just as good as the $400 software, and Rosetta Stone doesn't prompt users to go back to earlier segments over time.Duolingo also has a unique system where language learners help translate webpages (often Wikipedia) from their native language to the one they're learning, and will direct users to a level-appropriate page. This is a great way to see the language in a larger context, and helps give that feeling of confidence and mastery of the language.

column2: The kids love it! FUN and EDUCATIONAL!
column3: A friend recently showed me this app, and I am using it now for almost everyone in our family!  Learning Spanish has never been so much fun!  It's a great way to learn, having to say it, spell it, read it, hear it, and type it.  We've had many laughs repeating the Spanish sentences in different accents (Southern, Texan, etc)  as we are learning it, playing around as we are learning! (Something my son came up with to entertain himself while learning!)If you are learning Spanish, I would definitely give this a try.  Even as an adult, I loved the sound of the "correct" answers and earning my points and hearts! :)

column2: Great for Vocabulary, but Not for Grammar
column3: This app is an excellent resource for a huge selection of languages, which is a great thing of course! It is spectacular for learning at your own pace and teaching vocabulary, but it falls somewhat short for grammar. Duolingo needs to improve on explaining exceptions to rules of languages or just those rules themselves. Grammar is a key concept in language learning and the lack of a good way to teach it on this app is very disappointing.

column2: Don't think any more - get it now!

It's promised to be free forever but it would be worth paying quite a bit for it.I've been working with it for just over 2 months having emigrated to Italy and reached level 11. column2: Fun and free! Not a ripoff like many "free" programs
column3: I love using this app! I took this foreign language in college but haven't used it til now. Duolingo is an excellent refresher AND is teaching me more than I learned in college!

This is such a great app and I can't believe it's totally free - I love it!!!It teaches through a variety of methods, all intertwined to really immerse your brain in the learning process. For instance, I'm currently learning Spanish; I have to select correct photos with the Spanish word identifying them, translate Spanish phrases into English and vice versa, speak Spanish phrases to see if my pronunciation is correct, etc. This app reminds me a lot of Rosetta Stone (I was able to use that program for a time through a former employer) but a little less overwhelming; each lesson is very short and sweet meaning you'll actually do them (I remember dreading - and eventually stopping altogether - the RS lessons because each was at least a solid hour commitment each day which is a total buzzkill when you factor in work, social, and volunteer time). So, you can do one short lesson or if you've got the time breeze through several...the app views either as an accomplishment. And I love the owl reminders in my inbox each day because seriously: I can be a space case.This is a solid app for anyone wanting to learn a conversational foreign language, which is really the point, right? I mean, all I want to be able to do is communicate with other human beings in the language of the country in which I'm traveling (without an electronic translator!); who cares if I'm able to conjugate my verbs correctly every time I say something? I'm looking forward to learning a few languages with Duolingo!:)

Duolingo is hands down the best app for learning a different language. It's fun, educational, and very easy to learn. Plus, it doesn't cost an arm and a leg. column2: Duolingo is a fun way to learn a language

column2: Good Concept- but slow and cumbersome.

I've been using the app to study French for a few days now and I'm really enjoying it. I have used Rosetta stone in the past and I think this is pretty comparable.  There aren't structured grammar lessons, you just jump in, start translating and learn by doing.  It's easy to use and fun!

column2: This app is wonderful. It is enjoyable and actually helps you learn ...

I've found Duolingo to be an excellent tool for brushing up on my French. column2: Best Language App I've Found So Far.
column3: Cannot say enough good things about this app.  A fun, interactive way to learn and practice new languages.  I've learned (and retained) more Spanish with DuoLingo than I did in two years of high school and college Spanish.  And, it's useful Spanish... not the typical "at the restaurant", "at the hotel", "at the train station" sentences that I learn from many programs.  Previously learned words are incorporated into later sentences to help you learn and retain them.  Multiple languages are available... Spanish, Italian, French, German, Dutch, Danish, Irish, and others.I like that DuoLingo allows you to practice English to Spanish. Spanish to English, translation from written words and translation from sudio (occasionally difficult to recognize, but it does come with a "slow" option that phrases the sentence word by word instead of the rapid pace of a native speaker.  I would recommend that you also visit the DuoLingo.com webpage on occasion as it allows you to access sections like "Tips and Notes" that did not seem to be available from the app.Please note that DuoLingo does not actually provide "lessons."  It's more a learn as you go.  You can read the tips sections or just jump straight into practice sentences, but each sentence has a link to a "discussion" section where other Duo users (native speakers of either language) can help explain confusing grammar aspects.  I really enjoy the variety of "testing"... from translating pictures, to multiple choice, to picking the correct words out of an available group, or just typing in the translations without hints.  The web page also has the opportunity for "timed practice" so when you are reviewing lessons you feel you know well, you can set a thirty second timer and see how many translations you get right (extra seconds are added for each correct answer).Again, if I could give this app more stars I would.

column2: Fantastic free app; not perfect, but great value and tries to keep the learning interesting and varied
column3: For a free app, I was blown away by the value.You start by taking a sort of placement test.  After that, you're introduced to the "tree" of available subjects, in which you focus on one part of speech or related group of words: "Pronouns" or "Science" or "Past Present" or "Numbers".  These are collected in rows, and you have to finish all of the subjects in a row before you can move onto the next.Each subject consists of several "lessons", usually between 3 and 8.  You can work through the lessons one by one, and you'll be able to access definitions of words you don't know to help you learn.  Once you've completed all the lessons, you've finished the subject -- for now.  There is an alternative path to completion:  if you feel confident about the subject, you can "Test Out" by taking one roughly 20-question exam, and as long as you don't get more than 3 questions wrong, you can complete the subject that way, too.As you start filling in the tree, subjects you've already completed will open up again, so you have to keep going back to previous subjects to practice them and learn new vocabulary.  It's an effective way to keep you from "learning" something just long enough to finish the subject, but not really retaining the information.A word on the lessons themselves:  they're fairly varied.  I'm a native English speaker working on the Spanish tree, and I get questions where I have to translate a phrase or sentence from Spanish to English or from English to Spanish; spoken English where I have to type the Spanish translation and vice versa; spoken Spanish where I have to repeat it in Spanish; match-Spanish-words-to-English-definitions sets; and "choose all correct translations" multiple-choice questions.  In addition, you can access a kind of comments section for each question, where other Duolingo users post tips, comments, questions, and explanations.  You can also flag a question if you think it has an issue, and Duolingo reviews these and makes periodic updates.To up the fun factor, you earn "lingots" as you complete lessons, which you can use in the store to buy various add-ons.  You can also see your friends' progress, and a little competition can help keep you motivated!  You can also set daily email reminders and edit your goals to keep yourself on track.Overall, it's been a great way for me to refresh and improve my Spanish, which I haven't used in over ten years.

column2: Perfect freeware for learning a language
column3: This is really well done.  The game format makes it fun to learn a language.  The lessons are small enough that one can learn a little while in commute or in bed.The lessons are structured in a way that they build upon previous learnings and review them in the process.The software is well written in that it will call you out on a real mistake (gender of a noun, incorrect conjugation) but it let a minor spelling mistake or missing accent slide.There are some studies online showing how effective Duolingo is versus a college course.  After some time with the program, I'm convinced that's true.

Great app! I originally downloaded this app to learn Portuguese in order to talk to my Brazilian roommate's family. After two weeks I was able to translate some song lyrics and understand parts of conversations that my roommate had with her boyfriend. I am most of the way through the Portuguese language tree and still loving it. Now I am planning to use it to learn a few other languages, as well.Some cons (possibly specific to Portuguese): The translations are not exact, so knowing some Spanish or Italian is helpful for learning the grammar rules. Also, the pronunciations are a little odd because of the computer voice; they are sometimes hard to understand and do not give you a good idea for how to say the words (e.g., "de" is pronounced like "jay" in the app, but native speakers say it more like "jee"). Listening to native speakers and doing some reading in addition to using the app would be best, but Duolingo is an EXCELLENT place to start (especially if you don't want to or cannot take a formal class).Some pros: You can report any errors in the translations and they get taken care of pretty quickly (one that I reported was cleared up within a day). Each question in the app also has a comment option where you can ask questions; there are native speakers who monitor the forums and can respond to your questions relatively quickly. There is also an online component that is really good for working on spelling. The website that is connected to your account for the app also keeps an index of all the words you have learned and has explanations about grammar rules. Finally, in the app, unlike on the web version of Duolingo, you can turn on voice recognition if you want to work on you pronunciation.Some additional notes: The sentences are created by an algorithm based on the words you have already learned. As a result, they can be a little odd (e.g., "A borboleta escreve um livro" means "The butterfly writes a book"). Some people don't like this about the app, but I think it's entertaining.Overall, I love the app! Even with some of the cons, I still give it 5/5!

Don't get me wrong - I am thankful for free apps like Duolingo to help me learn beginning spanish. But after emerging into indirect pronouns, I see why so many people I have met through the years have only mastered declarative statements and simple questions.This is how spanish really is: the beginning is a little steep, like inching your way down that incline in the swimming pool. You know there's deep water somewhere in your future but you feel safe, as you're taking it in tiny tiny increments.Then you graduate, with absolutely no preparation whatever, into indirect pronouns. You slip off that shelf in the pool and suddenly you're in deep water. Nothing makes sense. And the sad thing is that Duolingo has not prepared you at all with ANY education about it.I have been studying spanish for years and got to this point in a couple of weeks. I have had to go to external sites to get the information I need about this.Duolingo is great but they need some in-depth education about hard things like indirect pronouns, where EVERY sentence is structured ENTIRELY different than in English.

It is 100% FREE!A few downfalls: 1 - the curriculum structure kind of befuddles me... some of the basics that are taught in classroom level 1 are last on the list here. 2 - sometimes a bit of explanation would be nice of a sentence structure or verb conjugation, or other basic notes are not explained and it is left up to the social aspect... 3 - I need to figure out how to turn off the notifications of someone else commenting in the social part, even months after I have. 4 - a few of the pronunciations need to be clearer. 5 - it doesn't always take in consideration spelling nor grammar errors.What else I would like to see added with a new update are more "game" like options during the learning process. A recent update added match the words. Absolutely brilliant. The update also included a proficiency percentage. I LOVE that! Oh, and the lingots, more options, please! column2: Fun and a great balance of easy + challenging!
column3: I downloaded this after trying several other, free "learn a foreign language" apps.The others were so frustrating, I mentioned the problem to friends, and - thank heavens - someone recommended Duolingo.I was skeptical at first, but once I got into Duolingo's lessons, I realized they really do work. They're exactly what I needed.I'd learned French in school, many years ago. I haven't spoken French in over 10 years, and only now and then recall it when I'm watching a French film with subtitles, or watching a Poirot mystery where it helps to know what he's muttering in French.Now, with a neighbor who speaks no English and our own planned move abroad, I need to refresh my French language skills. I'm starting from a point of recognizing a few words and phrases, but I couldn't say more than "Parlez vous..." ("Do you speak...") or "Je m'appelle..." ("My name is/I call myself...").So, I'm starting French again, not quite from scratch... but close enough.Duolingo is perfect for me. It's fun. It's light. It's free (though there may be ads on it, according to some reviewers), and I quickly learned: Pay attention during the easy lessons, because a challenge may be ahead. You'll need to remember those words and spellings.So far, the only reason I'd pay for the Plus version is because I want to support Duolingo. I love it that they provide these great lessons in basic French, free to everyone.I'm giving this an enthusiastic five stars. It's a light, fun course that feels more like play than serious study. But it still produces great results and learning.

column2: Great value, vocab and listening comprehension
column3: This app is primarily focused on learning vocabulary, learning increasingly complex grammar via translation, and listening to and transcribing native speakers. The module format keeps it from being overwhelming, and there's a good sense of progress. It won't make you fluent, but will give you enough of a background to go on to other resources, like reading a newspaper or conversing with native speakers. It also helps keep vocab sharp for languages not used in a while. For a free app, the amount you get is amazing.
Having trouble in pronunciation, but I enjoy learning and reading spanish

Free and fun! Very user-friendly. And no ads! Pretty much every win on this one. Would love to see them add a friend's talking option, but the instructional but in That might be trucky. It's a great app!

The best part, is it's not just one method... you have to translate Spanish to English, you have to translate English to Spanish, translate what you hear, and translate what you see.  Plus, if you get it on your phone you can do the audio part (on my kindle I had to change settings to opt out of this feature) where you actually have to speak Spanish out loud!  And moving between two devices works - it still tracks your progress! Lessons are short, and they stick.  I have no real reason to learn Spanish, other than it's just something to do, and I crave doing it like any other fun game app I have!

This FREE language learning course gives bite-sized lessons. Each lesson consists of a series of sentences teaching one area. You either translate into French, translate into English, or speak what the speaker has just spoken. The program passes or fails you on each response. There are several differences between the smart phone/tablet app and doing it on-line using a laptop. In the laptop program you cannot go on until you get the pronunciation mostly correct. In the app version after two attempts it moves on. In the laptop version when you translate from French into English you have to spell every word. In the app version the words are at the bottom, scrambled, with one extra word and you pick them one at a time to form a sentence. When you translate English into French you have to spell every word in both versions. The laptop version is better but the app works if you don't have a laptop with you. The same user name and password you use on the laptop will take you to the correct place in the app. I used it with an Amazon Fire HD 6 and Bluetooth headphones because linking the headphones with the Fire was easy and inking the headphones with Windows 8.1 is beyond my technical capabilities. column2: I am I right to give 4 stars?
column3: I would like to give this 5 stars, but I can't and am pressed to give it more than 2. While I applaud the attempt it has some major shortcomings. When trying to learn Chinese It is unclear to the English novice speaker if it is Mandarin, Cantonese, pinyin (?) or what. Then it asks you to type in the Chinese translation, but presents only an English QWERTY keyboard. Second, there is no way to go back it you accidentally make a wrong selection from the word choices. There is no verbalization of the Chinese words that are shown on the screen. This is not so bad with, say, French, where the phonics are similar (even though not the same), but with Chinese, Korean, etc. it is a drag and it makes learning MUCH more difficult. Notwithstanding these shortcomings, I think iyou can learn something if you struggle with it. But it shouldn't be a struggle.I am giving 4 stars for effort, but feel much work is needed to make the app user friendly. Duolingo is currently offered to students of Spanish, French, German, Italian, Portuguese, Dutch, Irish, Russian, Turkish, Polish, Hungarian and Romanian. I have worked with Duolingo's French program on and off for several years, so I can say from experience that it just keeps getting better and better. There are a few bugs, particularly in the recorded words, phrases and sentences, but there is also the capacity to give feedback when something does not sound right, or when the program is too rigid in its interpretation of "the" correct answer. There is a lively discussion group  among students, and this helps to resolve misunderstandings when they arise, as well as serve as another feedback mechanism for the developers. There are passages in the students' target language to work on translating, which range from Wikipedia entries to novels, and here crowd-sourcing really comes into play, as the finished products are being prepared for upload to the web. If working with a language you have not studied previously, I find it can be helpful to have an introductory text to the language to consult, but even that is not necessary, as there are valuable supplementary materials to be found online (e.g., at the about dot com sites for each language.)I have recently been working with the German and Italian programs, and I am enjoying them as much as I do the French. These programs can definitely become addictive, but in the best way possible, as the learner sees her/himself making progress in reading, writing and speaking the language, even one which may have been studied for years. And I haven't even mentioned the fact that this fascinating program is free! And that it moves seamlessly between the computer, smart phone and Kindle Fire!  I am waiting, along with many others, for the long-promised unveiling of the Chinese program.

column2: English to Spanish has lots of material and starts simply
column3: Based on Duolingo's rating system, I am an advanced Spanish-language learner. I got this free app hoping to brush up on my very rusty Spanish skills. For this purpose, I have been very grateful for the option to test out of each of the first three levels, and then to test out of each individual subject after that. I haven't yet reached a section test that I can't pass, but I've been studying Spanish ever since elementary school. Taking the tests provides a decent review, but I'm not sure it will help my conversational Spanish much.I certainly hope that the sections I haven't reached will cover the subjunctive as well as the future and conditional tenses. I haven't seen anything in the vosotros form either, so this may not be the best way to learn the Spanish spoken in Spain.  The vocabulary is very text-book style. There don't seem to be any words specific to a certain region or even any colloquial phrases included. I haven't seen any cultural notes, either. Those are not necessary for an introduction to the language, I suppose.It looks to me like the lessons begin very simply and build very gradually, so it would be an excellent choice for a beginner. I'm not sure yet how far it will take you into the more advanced grammar.  It probably doesn't help with conversational Spanish, but a person-to-person setting is the best for that anyway.I'm glad I've had the chance to try this out. I think I'll get a taste for French or German next!

column3: I've only just started using this app, but find it pretty good thus far.Seems like it teaches you the way you would learn a language organically, through trial and error correction.  I know, through past language study, that Duolingo is, through that trial and error process, teaching you how to use formal/familiar, male/female, singular/plural, and the like, constructions.  But, it's very subtle if you didn't have a clue about theses sort of things.That leads me to one of it's shortcomings, at least for me, and the reason the app is a 4 and not a 5.  Namely, it doesn't provide a whisper of explanation of these sorts of things.  It would be a great help, for me anyway, if the little message that pops up when you make an error gave an explanation.  For example, you have (no pun intended) tu, usted, vosotros, and ustedes, which all mean you.  Now in English there's just "you," no (in order) singular informal/formal or plural informal/formal versions of you, though generally we figure that out through context.  So a simple, "you used tu (the familiar),when you should have used usted (the formal)"  would be helpful in my being able to separate the two in my head.  And, go a step further and give me an easy place to find that tells me when I should use one over the other.In the vein of more explanations, please; How about explaining (in an initial page?) what xp points are and how they are used.  Or the meter that goes around the microphone; is more better?  I tried really butchering a phrase and pretty much got the same reaction. If more is better, then I could aim for that.

I have to say that I am honestly amazed that this application. After all, it was free.However, (bet you didn't see the "however" coming) this simple program uses all the latest techniques for teaching a language. You can also download, again for free, a variety of languages.It uses what is generally referred to as an "immersive" method of teaching. Because of this it's essential that you have the ability to speak to your phone or tablet into a microphone and be able to listen to what the program says to you. But in this day and age I don't know of any phone or tablet that doesn't have a microphone and speakers.With the immersive method of teaching there is no long explanation in English (say you're learning French or Spanish). Instead you are presented with a variety of pictures such as a little boy or a little girl, and adult man or woman, dog or cat or dog and cat or any of what seems like hundreds of combinations on screen at a time. Well, you never see more than a few different blocks with different pictures inside of each of them and they contain the label in the native language you're looking to learn. A prerecorded voice will say the name of each object in the new language. Then quiz time starts.It starts by showing you individual graphics that you had just seen, for example the young girl, and you are presented with a variety of terms in the native language and have to choose the one that represents the young girl. Of course it tells you if you're right or wrong but there are no harsh buzzers that go off or anything that makes you feel stupid. After all, you are learning a new language. The process continues and you will be presented with other images and choices to identify them.But the application doesn't just give you a collection of words. After you attain a high enough score showing that you now know the words for the pictures you've been shown the program shows you how to string them together in meaningful sentences using the correct grammar. The final step, just to make sure you've grasped what it is teaching you, is to speak into the microphone of your device (in say, Spanish if that's the language you're learning) and the program either moves on or goes back a short way in the lesson if your pronunciation is off.Not only am I learning both Spanish and French using this program but just to make sure I'm not wasting my time I showed both programs to people who speak those languages natively. I also strung together a few sentences from what I've learned so far and was told that both the grammar and pronunciation are correct.As all reviews should end the question should be asked, "would I recommend this to a friend?" If you haven't gotten it from my review, the answer is an outstanding "YES"! I can honestly say I've never given ANY program such a positive, enthusiastic review. As a final side note, the method used here for teaching is the exact same method used by a program called Rosetta Stone. This tiny little app was free and still is as of the time of this review (April 9, 2014), to learn a single language using the Rosetta Stone program just at this level could easily cost you a couple hundred dollars. Thus the enthusiasm.

column2: Very good app., but sometimes frustrating
column3: I enjoy using Duolingo, but like learning anything it can be very frustrating.  For example they wanted me to translate the sentence "She is unwell." from Spanish to English.  The first time I got it wrong because I didn't know the Spanish for unwell.  On strengthening the lesson, I got it right.  The next time I had the same sentence I decided to see how much leeway there was by saying, "She is not well."  They said it was wrong.  Now, I know that strictly speaking there was probably a different combination of words to state that specific sentence, but that seems to be nitpicking.  Sometimes you will be told something is right and other times it is wrong.  When speaking, there are times when I know I say the phrase correctly and they keep saying it doesn't sound right, and will eventually pass on to the next question.  Other times they will say it was right when I know that I screwed it up.  So, in conclusion, I still give them four stars because you can connect to other people who will explain things to you.

column2: Learn another language: all it costs is your time
column3: I have used Duolingo on other platforms: iOS and via a we b browser. You really can't fault them for much since the whole thing is FREE and is really well done. My wife picked up enough French in a few weeks a couple of years ago to be able to communicate in Paris, so I think that says a lot (about the software or about her, I am not certain. Maybe both!)I'd like to see it offer other languages... Japanese would be nice, but there is an impressive list available already, even for non-English speakers who want to learn other languages, including English. The format is a lot more like immersion and repetition than sitting in a classroom or reading a book, memorizing tables and rules. My only complaint so far is that I like to understand WHY an answer is correct or incorrect so that I can use the "rules" to make better decisions in the future. Maybe that is the wrong way to look at learning languages, but that's where I am. I've always had a hard time with vocabulary, but this approach seems to be helping.

I have chosen to learn spanish. I have friends who speak it and I see the written Spanish language around me every day, so this is helpful.  The lessons are broken down into small chapters, so you can determine your own speed.  If you lose all the hearts during the lesson, it means you need to repeat it.  You can even go back to lessons you mastered in the past to refresh your comprehension.  Also, if you need help in understanding a concept, you can read the notes and comments from other students and assistants (??) regarding that specific drill.  I also like to listen to the speaker and repeat the phrases even when the app does not require me to speak.  I also like to try to understand thephrases before peeking at the hints.  A nice interactive app which I downloaded for free which is very valuable.  I don't know if it eventually want me to pay to go farther in the future, but I will see how far I can go. I recommend this to beginners, those who want to get some basics on these languages offered, and old students who need a refresher.  Eventually, I will also check out the German lessons to see how much I have retained from high school 30 years ago.

column2: By far the best language app I've ever used
column3: I've been using Duolingo to improve my French.Over the years I've used a variety of language apps, podcasts, websites, books, and other resources to learn, or try to learn, a new language. Usually French or Cantonese. Duolingo is comprehensive in that it incorporates speaking, listening, and writing a language. My French had improved drastically just in the short time I've been using the app.The app addresses things that may seem minor, such as, allowing you to easily change your keyboard setting from English to French and back, and using the microphone to provide feedback on whether you are pronouncing things correctly. While I've found the microphone isn't always accurate, it's pretty good and definitely better than just speaking to an empty room with no feedback at all.I was disappointed that the app has so few languages available but I suspect this is what has allowed them to do so well with what they do offer. It also lacks instruction for people brand new to a language. While I had the benefit of having had some past instruction in the language, other people might find understanding the difference in sentence structures and how gender influences words, etc.Overall though I am very happy with it!

column2: Good if you cannot purchase Rosetta Stone.
column3: If you cannot pay for Rosetta Stone to learn a language, then this is for you.  It has several different methods of learning.  Each section has pictures to match words to; sentences to match from your current language to another; multiple choice questions; and dictation.  Examples of sections are the basics, food, animals, colors, etc. You have the option of reviewing each section (recommended) to retain your skill.  If you have a microphone, then the dictation section can be answered verbally.  This will help you with pronouncing the words correctly.  Check the available languages to see if the one you want to learn is there.  If not check back, because they are adding new languages.  And YES to the question on everyone's mind.  It is free.  The software keeps you at the same spot on all your devices.  For example, if I do several sections on the computer and open it on my Kindle (while connected to the Internet) it will update the Kindle app to what I just competed.

column2: A Very Useful App for Learning or Refreshing One's Ability in Various Languages
column3: I rarely actually use the apps that I download.  I'm bilingual and speak Spanish and English.  Spanish is my second language.  I became fluent while living in a Spanish speaking country for a couple of years.  Fast forward several decades and while I can still understand almost everything I hear in Spanish, my vocabulary has suffered, making it difficult to carry on a conversation for any length of time.Duolingo is far from perfect but it seems to be coded quite well.  I do get upset when I believe my answer or choice was correct and duolingo says it is wrong, but sometimes there are a great many ways to say something and it wouldn't be reasonable to expect Duolingo to always get it right.  It does seem to get it right most of the time, though, and I believe that if I'm able to persist in using this app for 10 minutes a day I might just find my vocabulary returning which I would appreciate very much.
This is a really fun way to learn some basics and decide if you want to further your study of a foreign language.

I tried this on a whim because it was free. I didn't expect it to be so good. I think it is better than the Rosetta Stone Russian that I had been doing awhile back and stopped because I became frustrated because it would take awhile to figure out what I did wrong because they wouldn't tell me. When you make a mistake, this app tells you what you did wrong. The only problem I have is that I am doing it on the first generation Kindle Fire and it doesn't have an international keyboard as far as I know. I am doing German, since Russian is not offered yet on Duolingo, and I get some of the writing questions wrong because I don't use umlauts which I can't use because I don't have the keyboard.

The app is well-designed and makes practicing a language fun rather than just repetitive. It teaches not only vocabulary, but content and structure as well. I've learned as much Spanish in a week of using this app as I did in several years of high school and college classes. It's a 5 star app except that it "freezes" fairly often and requires me to restart my Kindle.

This is a great app to use when learning a language. The only two problems I have with it is that it sometimes does not recognize what you say and the little lessons do not have the written explanation that the website has.

column2: Great Beginners App, but Better Maintenance App
column3: You've heard the saying, 'If you don't use it,  you lose it.' This is true for innumerable things, but never more so than in languages. This app helps me maintain my language proficiency, and if you know the process for language learning can jumpstart additional languages. I would recommend caution to those who have no experience whatsoever in languages though. Depending on the person's independent learning level this might not be the best introduction to languages.I would like to see more languages, including some that are more academic in nature; Classical Latin, Attic/ Classical Greek, Classical Hebrew or even modern Hebrew, and maybe some Arabic and/or Farsi.

This is a great way to practice a language on your own. I tried it to learn french and have learned quite a bit in just a week. It has reminders to keep you on track if you are busy all the time. Best of all it is free!

column2: fun and accessible way to learn a language

column2: Fun and effective way to learn
column3: Duolingo is fun to use. It's got a clean, attractive interface that's easy to use. It's been reliable and consistent for me, and I've rarely had any issues with it. Overall, Duolingo is a high-quality and effective product, and--surprisingly--free.I'm looking forward to continuing my study of Spanish. Currently, my favorite online resources are "News in Slow Spanish - Latino", Superflashcard.com, and of course Duolingo. ¡Adelante!

column2: One of the best free language apps out there!
column3: I absolutely LOVE this app! It is easy, fun to use, creative, and very well put together. I've only had it for a week and have already improved my conversational French by a lot.Each level gives you multiple things to strengthen your knowledge of the language. Like spelling the words, or selecting pictures, to hear it verbally repeated. And then the function of turning off your mic is very nice but I highly recommend taking every opportunity you can to use the voice program and saying the words and phrases out loud, it was very eye-opening to see when I was saying something wrong.The only draw back to this program is that it will introduce a new word and not tell you why you have to use it instead of another one (Les vs. Le), I figured it out on my own from my past knowledge of French, but if I was just beginning it might be confusing.I would highly recommend this to anyone wanting to freshen up on a language or learn something new!

column2: Really fun way to learn a new language

The forms you use are to listen/read and identify by speaking, typing, translating from Spanish to English and vice-versa. If there was a way to give it 4 and 1/2 stars, I would have. column2: A great platform to start a new language

Love, love this app! My Spanish speaking skills are limited to say the least. (Been a long time since high school. And no, you can't ask how many years!) So when my son told me about Duolingo, I was skeptical. But it is great! I am beginning to understand not only words, but grammar as well. (Although I am still struggling with plurals and pronouns!)Duolingo uses auditory, visual, and traditional methods of learning a language. There is some memorization but the lessons are integrated with hearing the words/sentences spoken, and pictures. You build on one lesson to the next. and if you fail to grasp the concepts, then OOPS! you have to start over. While my Spanish instructor friends may frown upon this "shortcut" method, it is providing me with the rudimentary skills to perhaps pursue a higher level of learning Española. I like that it is available for my phone, Kindle Fire or PC, so there's no excuse for not doing today's lesson. Now if I can just get those durn plurals and pronouns correct. Adios, mi amigos/amigas!

column2: More than just a way to learn a language free....
column3: If you don't know about Duolingo, you should probably research it some.  It is so much more than a way to learn a new language for free.  This is a top quality program that will teach you to speak a major language in the style of Rosetta Stone.  It isn't exactly like Rosetta Stone and there aren't nearly as many languages, but it is free AND it is for a good cause.  The back story on Duolingo is that once you have reached a specific level of ability, you actually begin to translate books and websites.  You see, computers are really not very good at translation, but people are.  Once you are proficient enough, you will be translating actual webpages.  Your translation will be compared with hundreds of others to find what is correct (computers are good at this part).  Don't believe me?  Go to Duoling dot com and check it out.  Not only will you pick up a super helpful skill but you will give back to humanity at the same time.

I love this program. It incorporates all aspects of the language; vocabulary, spelling, grammar and diction. Each lesson introduces you to a specific part of the language (i.e basics, food, animals, pronouns, verbs, possessions, ect.) and test/teaches you in various ways. It includes pictures asking you to identify words to sentence translation to auditory exercises asking you to type what you hear as well as a voice recognition utilizing your tablet's microphone to test your diction. I especially love the play back feature on various exercises, which allows you to listen to a native speaker and practice modeling after them.I have tried a variety of free language apps and this one is superior by far. My only complaint is the "bonus" lessons you can obtain as you build "xp" are far more advanced than the language you have learned thus far through the regular lessons. However, if you re-visit these bonus lessons after progressing further through regular lessons, they begin to make more sense.As with any language app, you have to be willing to put the work in. You are learning a new language after all. If you approach this app with the expectation that it will take hard work and diligence to learn and master a new language, this will be the perfect teaching tool for you.

column2: Bite-sized daily lessons mix variety and repetition
column3: I studied French in high school and college years ago, and I've picked up a bit of Spanish here and there, and by reading some of the Bible in Spanish. I decided to pick up some German with Duolingo because I have a nephew who studied that. Well, that started out so well I decided to brush up my French and see what I could do with Spanish. Probably not a good idea to work on three languages at once, but I'm enjoying it and making progress. I was so rusty on French my attempt to test out of the Basics failed (just barely), but it's nice to know the option is there if you don't want to review from the beginning. Repetition is an important part of learning any language, but it can get boring. This program solves the problem by mixing up the styles of questions. It starts out very easy - some of the questions are as easy as tapping the picture of the word given in your native language with the target language below it. On some questions, you can tap the given word and see its translation, so you don't have to guess even if it is a new word (but guessing can be fun and doesn't "hurt" much!). Pay attention to the little words that go with them, though! In English (which is hard to learn in other ways) we just have "the" for everything, but in French and Spanish you have variations to match the gender and number of the objects (German has three singular forms, one being neuter, I guess). How do you know if an object takes a masculine (le or el) or feminine (la)? Practice, practice, practice! Take your time and think and memorize, and write words and combinations down. And Duolingo does let you go back and review skill sets. The instant feedback is much more enjoyable than doing written homework, but the German is making me want to get a textbook and do some extra studying! Some questions let you translate phrases or sentences by selecting from a choice of words, others let you listen to spoken words, phrases, or sentences and then select the words you hear. More challenging questions require you to type in the translation or words from memory. It even has voice recognition so some questions require you to repeat things in the target language. If it doesn't recognize what you say, it doesn't count it against you (lots of things can go wrong with voice recognition, such as background noises). If you can't get away from the noise or otherwise can't or don't want to use your microphone, you can turn off that feature and it will only give you the other kinds of questions. I've noticed that it also gives some leeway for typographical errors, although sometimes it's still counted typos as wrong and other times I've just been wrong but it was counted as a typo. It generally gets it right and the two kinds of errors balance out. I've typed in a translation when the task was to type out what was spoken in the foreign language, and it gave me a do-over. But watch out, if you make a mistake in your own language, it will count that wrong, too! English speakers had better know how to properly use "to," "too," and "two," for example. Or maybe using DuoLingo will help you with that, too! Daily e-mail reminders (which can be turned off) help you to stick to it.[ADDED LATER] Well, I'm up to Level 5 in all three languages, and I'm definitely feeling the pinch of trying to make it QuadLingo. As I fail lessons, though, previous skills re-open to show where I need to go back and practice more, which is a good thing. It's exciting to be learning these languages, and I'm thinking I might dig through my collection of language texts to add to and aid my DuoLingo studies, since I've gone and set myself a three-pronged challenge. I wish I'd thought of taking notes earlier (I just added that bit with this edit); I'm sure that would be enough to make studying one language a cinch with DuoLingo.

If I didn't count wrong and if all languages have the same lessons, there are 68 different desperate lessons you climb down a lesson path to and each has a related set of words. That probably didn't make much sense so sorry.I also really like the sense of community you get. With every answer, you can choose to "discuss" it (at least on the computer you can) and you'll see a bunch of others helping others out by commenting. You can reply, up vote, down vote, and even give a Lingot to those comments.That leads me to another topic. As a reward for completing various things, you get Lingot which is the online store's form of currency. With Lingots, you can purchase aids, aesthetics, and on the computer, even other random lessons like "Flirting." You can't buy Lingots and so the currency remains fair.On the computer, there's a few more things you can do other than complete lessons. I've been using this app on my 7" Kindle Fire HD and my HTC One SV for approximately a week... maybe a week and a half now, and I absolutely love it!I'm using it to learn German... not sure what other language options there are, although I know Spanish and French are in there. So far I am hugely impressed. The app uses a combination of written, spoken, and visual cues/questions... so one question may ask me to translate a sentence from German to English, the next question might be to translate something from English to German, and the question after that may be to speak a sentence in German or to write a sentence in German that the app speaks (the app's voice is not great, but definitely serviceable)... reinforced occasionally by visual cues such as labeled pictures (i.e. a picture of a dude labeled "der Mann"... you get the idea after a bit).The teaching method works, I have to say... and this from a guy who always considered himself critically handicapped when it came to learning new languages.  Granted, I'm early into the program, but I am retaining a large part of each lesson, which is honestly more than I can say for my experience with Rosetta Stone.There are two cons that I've noted: First, and this may have been an individual problem, the app wouldn't let me sign in with either Google+ or Facebook... it has buttons for doing that, but they didn't work... so I had to go old-school and actually create a separate account.  Minor glitch, but still worth noting.  The second con is that in the course of the lessons, I haven't yet encountered a definitive explanation of certain rules of grammar, i.e. when to use one form or another of a verb. On one hand this is vaguely annoying, as I end up with wrong answers without being entirely certain why they're wrong; on the other hand, however, I suspect that this is actually increasing the effectiveness of the program, as this makes me really think about each word before I use it, and when I'm wrong, I really study WHY I was wrong, which ultimately increases retention of the language. So kudos for effectiveness, even if it is a bit annoying.Overall... freaking awesome.  Get this app.  I can't believe it's free, honestly, but as long as it is, get it!

column2: Such a fun way to learn or reinforce a new language.
column3: My grandson introduced this system to me as an aid in augmenting my Rosetta Stone and Pimsleur Italian lessons and it helps a lot.  Rosetta Stone is a multi-pronged method that keeps you at the computer and can frustrate you if you don't pay a lot of attention to the proper spelling of the new language.  I am not interested in writing Italian and it is pretty easy to figure out close enough to read because it is such a phonic language but many words are blended and therefore difficult to separate for spelling purposes.  Pimsleur is all audio and I can listen to it in my car or at home so it gives me more flexibility from that standpoint.  Duolingo offers aids that act as reminders to help reinforce your learning and gives the explanations that are missing in Pimsleur.  Maybe it is me, but I find it helpful if I can see the conjugations of verbs to make those connections.  This also has a fun aspect to it so I find I resort to it when I have a few minutes here and there to devote.  Both Rosetta Stone and Pimsleur require a more disciplined approach that needs you to set time aside each day for language learning and reinforcement.  Best of all, it is FREE....how can you go wrong!

I got this app when I was first searching to get applications on my new device. I have been interested in learning german since middle school, and saw that you could learn it through this app for free! I was on break from classes so I had time and figured I'd give it a go. There is a ton to learn and lessons are divided into very bite size segments.I know that the app tries to immerse you into the language and that is great. My complaint is that it is completely guess and check. Some questions are easy to decipher while on others I had to blindly guess or not put an answer. There is no instruction, not even basic grammar hints. You figure it out on your own. Like I said, this approach is good...to a certain extent. When things that "should" work don't, it can be frustrating. There is an option to comment on questions and looking through previous questions you can usually figure out where you went wrong. This is a helpful feature. This app would be great if it would give you some information on basic grammar or rules though. If they used immersion with some mini lessons squeezed between, this app would be phenomenal.I am about half way through and have decided to get some books to really learn the language (more vocab, sentences, etc and grammar because this app is lacking there). Thankful for this app though. It's given me a small background in the language so I won't be a total newbie when I start my studies. I am sure I will continue to use this application and may even go through it again once I have more of a german foundation. I'm sure I'll have several "ah ha!" moments.

I have been using this app for a few months now, and at first glance, I thought it was fantastic, but I think that was because I was fervidly learning the German language because of my strong desire to do so, it is also because prior to starting Duolingo, I developed a partial understanding of the language through a variety of sources, to be honest, I don't think Duolingo is a good way to learn a language.One of the reasons being is that it was easy to understand as far as my previously developed understanding of the language, but when I was trying to learn new things in the language, it was difficult for me to learn regardless of my desire to learn the language, because Duolingo doesn't do much to teach you new things, all it does is tell you the definition of unknown words, and you have to rely on yourself to remember them.Another thing is that Duolingo doesn't teach the grammar of the language at all, and I know this because I understand that there are certain grammar rules in German that are different in English, I don't know exactly what those rules are, but I know they exist, and when I translate a sentence from English to German where the grammar rules apply, it is usually an incorrect translation, and I have no idea how to learn from my mistakes in this app, the only help you can get on this app is comments from other users of the app, which is only helpful sometimes.I think the only things this app can be used for is to get background information on subsequent education of the language, or to practice what you already know in the language. If your goal is to learn a language, this app shouldn't be used as your main source.

I have been working with Instant Immersion, on my computer for over a month, which I also feel is a good learning experience, but I feel that I have been learning a substantial amount from Duolingo. I wanted to learn how to conjugate verbs, so that I would feel more competant forming my own sentences. Duolingo has been teaching me how to do that, as well as building more of a vocabulary, and teaching me sentence structure, and commonly used phrases. I have only been using this app for a little over a week, but I feel that I have learned quite a bit from it in that relatively short amount of time.  There is still a long way to go, but I have noticed that as I complete more sessions, they begin to speak longer sentences, and more rapidly. I am thankful for the turtle button, as I an not always up to speed with them. I do realize that in the real world, people will not be speaking slowly.  I look forward to my learning sessions, and want to explore some of the other languages, once I feel competent with Spanish. I would highly recommend this for anyone sincerely wanting to be able to communicate in a language that they do not currently speak. I think that what I learn in this course will help me progress with the other language program, at a more rapid pace. My daughter and I will be traveling to Spain next year with her Spanish class, so not ever having learned Spanish previously, I am working hard, to try to become proficient in being able to communicate. I do not want to feel handicapped by my lack of knowledge of the native language. Thank you for the opportunity to use this app, especially at no charge.

column2: Better than my paid subscription to a language site
column3: Really does help you learn a language with practice. It quizzes you to verify your understanding. The process is engaging and ultimately inspires you to teach yourself without a physical teacher present. There are User Discussions associated with lessons, but I found myself doing additional Internet searches on certain words and phrases. The extra research significantly enhanced my understanding and helped me remember better.Also, there's a lot of fun to be had here. It offers multiple ways to learn (listening, speaking, writing and translating) which all serve to help you remember your new language. Plus, there is the "gaming" element that allows you to achieve points called "lingots" that can be traded for special learning modules. I gave this app 4 stars instead of 5 because it sometimes gave me "credit" for speaking the correct words when I had actually flubbed up the language. But for the most part, it was spot on!I actually have a paid subscription to a language learning site, but I find myself returning most often to this app.

column2: Just getting started but I love it so far.
column3: I have just started using this program but I like it so far.  There are several languages to chose from (I'm using Spanish and Irish) and I've been able to use the app on my kindle, iTunes, iPhone, and iPod. It would probably work on other systems too.  In addition, the program is very well rounded.  You are able to test out if you are familiar with the language you select.  Each lesson has matching, conjugation, spelling of words in each language, practicing the words out loud on a recorder, etc.  There is a lot offered for a free app.

column2: Brushing up on my language skills
column3: I down loaded this app to brush up on my foreign language skills starting with French. I had 8 years of French, about 60 years ago. So I thought to skip the basics and start of with the phrases. However, I could not understand the teacher's French accent. Maybe because I learned French in Holland, even though I spent every summer for six years in southern Belgium and one summer in Paris. To make a long story short, I had to start with the basics to get used to the teacher's voice and accent. Now about the app. I am happy I downloaded it, and working rapidly through the lessons. It is a great program, but I am not sure if the microphone on my Kindle Fire HDX is working or not, when it asks for pronunciation of the phrases. I'll have to figure that out later. I will add to my review later on some more, after I finish all the lessons. I plan to brush up on German next, and will check out what other languages I can learn.

column2: It's great, easy, fast and best of all free!
column3: It's not setup the way I was taught or would teach it, but the method used does work. I feel like it's more geared towards learning how to speak it, understand it and write it in as little time as possible. I guess what I'm trying to say is that in school you learn all the colors at once not in segments; however Duolingo, introduces one or two colors, a verb, a few animals, clothing and people all at once. Talk about remembering a lot all at once! But that's what the program does well; it introduces those new terms and makes you go over them multiple times to get it to sink in. Even when you go to the next lesson, you're still practicing a few terms from the last lesson!
So far the pace is excellent and I seem to be picking up the vocabulary pretty well.

column2: Very user friendly fun way to learn a language

column2: Pretty Good If Used with Other Materials
column3: I've been using a mobile version on my Android phone for a while. I assume this is the same. In some ways it's better than the website because it remembers what you got wrong and re-tests you at the end of a lesson. Sometimes that's what you need.On the other hand, it is hard to comment on this app without talking about the Duolingo method. The method is only really useful in conjunction with other language materials. It doesn't really teach anything, it just sort of throws words, phrases and sentences at you in a pseudo-random order in whatever context is being "taught". For vocabulary great, for learning a technical aspect of grammar, less so.On the third hand, it's free. How much complaining can a guy do?

The exercises really help whip my skills into shape in a way workbooks just can't--you can choose to continually practice the grammar and vocab with which you're not yet comfortable and breeze through (or even test out of) things you already know. I really appreciate the ability to connect with other users through the discussion threads, which contain excellent explanations and advice if you get stuck on a certain skill. Having the ability to practice translating articles from all over the web and have other users critique your work is also a plus, since it's the most practical experience you can get without, you know, actually speaking to another human in the target language. column3: I am at the very beginning of my journey to learn French, and this free app has made it fun and enjoyable for me.  This app starts you off by jumping in with both feet. No instructions really, just trial and error right away and I was pleasantly surprised at how effective it was.  If you miss a phrase, a little word balloon will open up showing you the correction. The best part about the correction balloon is the link to a chat page where other people have already asked questions and the incredibly informative responses. I've learned a great deal about the grammar and foundation of the language just from reading these back and forth questions and answers.  You are encouraged to participate daily which isn't a problem for me as I look forward to it. As you progress you earn Lingots (I think that's what they're called)  which you can use to purchase little fun add-ons for the app. What I am very happy with is how much content they give you. For French I can see the lessons go on for quite a while, providing more and more detail about the language. I've tried listening to French audio files and have even tried a free preview of Rosetta stone, but nothing I've tried before has been as interesting and informative as the Duolingo app. Highly recommended and I hope you enjoy!

column2: Intuitive, Easy to Use, Great Between Devices
column3: This app is fantastic! I've been using it for weeks now to learn Spanish. The controls are intuitive and I find it easy to learn a second language. It's a great way to learn another language, and the best part is that it's 100% free. However, the one tiny issue that I have with this app is that you need to have speakers. This is fine when you're working on it at home, but in public places; not so much. It plays a word/phrase in whatever language you're learning, and you are supposed to type that word/phrase out. It's a bit awkward when one is in a quiet place (think waiting room at the doctor's office). You have to turn the volume way down and hold it up to your ear, or just wear headphones. This isn't a major issue, and all in all, I think that Duolingo is a fantastic app for people of all ages to learn an important life skill of being bilingual.

column2: Good, if you already know the basics
column3: I love this app. I use it to maintain and strengthen my Spanish skills; however, I do not find it very useful for learning entirely new languages. Instead of teaching rules and patterns, such as stem verbs, conjugations, etc., it requires the learner to memorize practically every aspect of the language down to the smallest details. In essence, there's no explanation of why. Why does the third person plural use this verb ending? Why do I use this past tense instead of that one (since in Spanish, there are two imperfect past tenses)? As a student of languages and their historical progression, I have found it crucial to teach languages according to rules, patterns, and conjugational conventions. This app, however, seems to overlook this extremely helpful principle. I had hoped to use Duolingo to continue learning German and begin learning Italian, but I will instead have to use a textbook to first learn all the necessary grammar rules and then use the app to practice and increase my vocabulary. Overall, it is a fairly solid aid to self-education.

column2: An excellent resource and it really is 100% free
column3: This is a great way to brush up on language skills.  I took Spanish in high school but made it my New Year's resolution to get back into it.  I love that this is totally free.  It encourages you to log in every day to practice the skills you've learned and add new ones.  It keeps track of your progress and can compare to friends who are also using the program.  It has a bunch of languages including Spanish, French, German and Italian and several others in the works like Turkish, Vietnamese and Polish.Each "lesson" incorporates translating from English, translating to English, speaking and listening exercises.  You can turn off the speaking and learning exercises.  I do. I find that it doesn't recognize my voice very well. I think part of that is my pronunciation and part of it is the voice recognition.Duolingo has both a mobile and online computer-based components.  You can use either one or both (all for free).  I like the computer version better.  It's easier to type on a real keyboard.  The PC version gives you more practice when you make an error, but the mobile version gives three chances before you fail the lesson and have to start over. I also like that the PC version has a translation mode and gives you an estimate of how much you can understand of the "real" language.There is a lot of pattern recognition and memorization involved.  There are some little tidbits in the lessons, but some things are very much missing.  I'm still trying to sort out "por" and "para" and trying to understand the personal "a."  (Feel free to comment with some hints).  Fortunately there are other web resources to back up this learning.I've almost finished the Spanish lessons.  I will probably work on Italian (while practicing Spanish) next.  It will be interesting to see if it's as helpful when I try a language that i have had no previous exposure to.

column2: The VERY BEST language learning app!
column3: I have had two years of French in school and used virtually every language program available. Here are my critiques:Rosetta Stone...didn't like that because it didn't present the material in a way that appealed to me or that stuck with me. Also, it frustrated me as it seemed disorganized and a backwards approach. Plus it's expensive. At least $400  for entire program. Pimsleur: it is pretty good actually. The one drawback to Pimsleur is that I sometimes can't understand exactly what they are saying, even after having two years of the language under my belt,  therefore, you don't get the concept of how the language is organized. Plus it is expensive. The pro to it though is that you can listen to the audio in your car or while cleaning house or jogging.FrenchPod: pros: you can download audio files to listen to wherever you are. The speakers have  a natural French dialog and then go over it bit by bit and explain the various uses of the words. You can alsodownload workbook pages to refer to.Cons: There us an extremely limited list of lessons, all of which are around 6 sentences to dissect. Also, there is no practice, either speaking or writing.Textbooks: Difficult. Boring.DuoLingo: pros:  you get to hear the audio spoken at a natural speed. Then you can slow it down so you can pick up on each word as it is enunciated. You are immersed in the language by having to type out, which forces you to remember placement of nouns and verbs etc.  It is formatted sort of like a game, so it doesn't feel much like work, and it is actually quite addictive. It's totally FREE! No ads either.Cons: it can get frustrating if you get an answer wrong because you miss points, so like with any "game," you might get frustrated if you're that serious about game points.I have learned FAR more with this app in 6  months than I EVER learned in all my previous years using other methods! It's fun and free and best of all...it works!!

column2: A little lacking, but otherwise good.
column3: I originally downloaded this app to help me brush up on my French, which is pretty rusty after 15 years of little to no use, and my Spanish, which is just a little rusty after a year of little to no use. I am somewhat pleased with this app. I don't like it as much as I like my French and Spanish classes, but as far as a language tutor, it's great. The only thing lacking in this app is that it doesn't explain the conjugations of verbs with respect to pronouns. For instance--and I'm going to use Spanish as an example here--it doesn't explain why the verb 'ser' gets conjugated to 'eres' when you say "tu eres," or why it gets conjugated to 'somos' when you say, "nosotros somos." If it explained the process of conjugation for each language, that would make the app SO MUCH better and also help newbies have a fuller understanding of the language they are trying to learn. Anyone who doesn't know the first thing about other languages is going to think that this app is great, but if you are like me and you have had formal classes before, you will know that this app is seriously lacking. Formal classes give you the fundamental principles of the language to help you, and one of those fundamentals is learning conjugation so that you will not only understand what you're saying, but WHY you're saying it that way. I know this app isn't the same as a formal class, but if the developers are going to market it as an alternative to expensive formal classes, then they need to at least offer better teaching tools within the app.

column2: One of the best language-learning apps I've seen so far
column3: This is an excellent app and an excellent website. I've been a language learner for over 40 years, and Duolingo is one of the best facilitators I've seen. It combines some of the best aspects of its predecessors, like Rosetta and Mango, but it's free (!), and it's very entertaining (it keeps you translating sentences like "I'm a horse, and I speak English"), and it reminds you when you need refresher work. I've only been using it for a short time, but it's excellent for learning the bones of a language. I don't think it's for the weekend traveler; it doesn't give you the hello/how are you stuff. It concentrates on vocabulary and grammar (in a fun non-schoolroom way). So, if you just want to learn Please and Thank you and How are you?, buy a phrasebook. If you're going to be in Norway / Spain / France / Germany for a month or so, try Duolingo. It will entertain you and educate you, and give you what you need.

I found the pedagogy a bit lacking. This year, I took advantage of their "back-to-school" half-off sale  and find it much improved -- the on-line version, anyway. The first part of a lesson is an overview of the material, then it is broken down into focusses on discrete skill areas - listening, grammar, reading and writing. Every two weeks, you get a 45-min. session with a tutor via a form of Skype.I haven't investigated the games function yet, since I haven't gotten that far. Like all learning products, it requires self-discipline and motivation,but the pacing of the materials keeps you going.Some, but rather few, of the pictures and graphics are culturally appropriate. I think for verbs and everyday activities, they use the same photos for all the languages.
